findings.title: Any date override on the slot's day short-circuits the busy-time check
findings.body: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, after the date-override loop, `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns availability immediately whenever a date override exists for the slot's day. This skips the `busy.every(...)` check below, so existing bookings, calendar busy times and buffers are completely ignored on days that have a date override, allowing double bookings on those days.

findings.title: Working-hours end boundary computed from slot start, ignoring event length
findings.body: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation instead of using `slotEndTime`. The check `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore never accounts for the event duration, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them is treated as available.

findings.title: Dayjs objects compared with === (always false)
findings.body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset,'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset,'minutes'))` compares two freshly created Dayjs object references, which is never true. The intent (detecting a zero-length override, i.e. a day marked unavailable) is never reached, so days blocked out via a start==end override are still offered as bookable.

findings.title: Date-override day comparison uses local-time formatting and a hand-rolled offset
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset,'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` parses the stored UTC override date in the server's local timezone and then shifts it by `dayjs.tz(date.start, organizerTimeZone).utcOffset() * -1`, which reinterprets the UTC instant as organizer wall time. The resulting day string can be off by one day depending on the server TZ, causing overrides to be matched to the wrong date (slots wrongly allowed/blocked). Use explicit `dayjs.utc(...)`/`.tz(organizerTimeZone)` conversions instead.

findings.title: Override timezone may be undefined and minute-of-day conversion drops day wrap
findings.body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `timeZone` typed optional (`TimeRange.timeZone?`); when it is undefined dayjs falls back to the local/system timezone, silently producing a wrong organizer offset. Additionally start/end are reduced to `hour()*60 + minute()` after applying the offset, so when the offset pushes the range across midnight (e.g. organizer 22:00-23:00 viewed from a +6h invitee tz) the computed endTime becomes smaller than startTime and the override yields no slots at all instead of the correct range.

findings.title: Spread order can overwrite the injected userId on date overrides
findings.body: `{ userId: availability.user.id, timeZone: availability.timeZone, ...override }` spreads the override last, so if an override object carries its own `userId` (the `TimeRange` type declares `userId?: number | null`) it overwrites the intended user id, breaking the per-user override matching in `getSlots`. Put the explicit fields after the spread.

findings.title: New test does not exercise the behaviour the PR fixes
findings.body: The added assertion calls getSchedule with `Asia/Dhaka` and expects exactly the same UTC slots as the `Asia/Kolkata` call, so it would also pass with the old (broken) override handling — it asserts nothing timezone-specific. Also, the PR's main claim (date overrides of fixed hosts being respected for ROUND_ROBIN events) has no test at all; a round-robin scenario with a fixed host override should be added.
